questions.title: Types of Dependency Injection
questions.question: What are the different types of dependency injection in Spring?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Three types:** constructor, setter, field injection
- **Constructor injection is preferred:** immutable, testable, no reflection hacks
- **Field injection (`@Autowired` on field) is the worst:** breaks unit testability without Spring
- **Spring team recommends constructor injection** since Spring 4.3 (no `@Autowired` needed for single constructor)
- **Red flag:** advocating for field injection — shows you haven't considered testability

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Spring supports three types of dependency injection: constructor, setter, and field injection.

Constructor injection is the recommended approach. Dependencies are passed as constructor parameters, making them mandatory and immutable once set. The class is honest about what it needs — you can see all dependencies at a glance. And crucially, you can instantiate the class in a plain unit test without Spring, just `new MyService(mockDep1, mockDep2)`.

Setter injection is for optional dependencies. You inject via a `@Autowired` setter method, which means the object can be created without the dependency and configured later. Useful for optional plugins or when you need to change a dependency after construction.

Field injection uses `@Autowired` directly on a field. It looks concise but it's the worst option — you can't inject dependencies without reflection, making unit testing painful. You either use Spring context in tests or use field injection workarounds. Avoid it for anything other than test classes.

sections.title: The Real Reason Constructor Injection Won
sections.content:
Most developers learn that Spring has three injection types and that constructor injection is "recommended." What they miss is **why** the Spring team changed their official stance — and what happens in production when you pick the wrong one.

Before Spring 4.x, the community was split. Field injection was popular because it looked clean — one annotation, no constructor boilerplate. Setter injection had its advocates for optional dependencies. But as codebases grew and teams tried to write unit tests without spinning up a full Spring context, the testability gap became impossible to ignore.

The fundamental issue is **object completeness**. With constructor injection, an object either has all its dependencies or it doesn't exist — there's no partially-constructed state. You can't accidentally call a method before a dependency is set. With field injection, an object exists first, then its fields are populated via reflection, creating a window where the object is alive but broken. That window causes NullPointerExceptions in tests, race conditions in lazy scenarios, and mysterious failures when someone refactors dependency order.

Spring 4.3 settled the debate by making `@Autowired` optional on single-constructor classes. This removed the last argument for field injection — boilerplate — and made constructor injection the path of least resistance.

sections.title: What Each Injection Type Actually Costs You
sections.content:
The three injection types differ on six dimensions that matter in real projects. Boilerplate is the only one where field injection wins — and Lombok eliminates even that advantage.

| Concern | Constructor | Setter | Field |
|---|---|---|---|
| Immutability | `final` fields, fully immutable | Mutable, can be reassigned | Mutable, set via reflection |
| Required vs optional | Compile-time enforcement | Runtime — `null` possible | Runtime — `null` possible |
| Unit testing | `new Service(mockA, mockB)` | Create object, then call setters | Requires reflection or Spring context |
| Circular dependency | Fails fast at startup | Silently allowed | Silently allowed |
| Readability | All deps visible in constructor signature | Scattered across setter methods | Scattered across fields |
| Boilerplate | Most verbose (mitigated by Lombok) | Moderate | Least verbose |

The circular dependency row deserves attention. Constructor injection makes cycles **impossible to ignore** — Spring throws `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException` at startup. Field and setter injection allow cycles silently by injecting partially-constructed references, which means the bug hides until a specific call order exposes it in production.

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Disambiguates when multiple beans of the same type exist:** the core use case
- **Takes a bean name:** matches the specific bean you want
- **Combined with `@Autowired`:** `@Qualifier` alone doesn't inject
- **Alternative: `@Primary`:** marks one bean as default winner without needing `@Qualifier` everywhere
- **Red flag:** not knowing `@Qualifier` works by bean name and `@Primary` makes one default

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
When you have multiple beans of the same type registered in the Spring context, `@Autowired` alone fails because Spring doesn't know which one to inject — it throws `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException`. `@Qualifier("beanName")` disambiguates by specifying exactly which bean you want by its name.

For example, if you have two `DataSource` beans — a primary and a read-replica — you'd annotate the injection point with `@Qualifier("primaryDataSource")` or `@Qualifier("replicaDataSource")` to get the right one.

The alternative is `@Primary` — you mark one bean as the default winner. When `@Autowired` finds multiple beans, it picks the `@Primary` one. Use `@Primary` when one implementation is the standard choice and `@Qualifier` for the others. This way, most code doesn't need `@Qualifier` at all.

sections.title: When Spring Finds Two Beans and Doesn't Know Which One You Want
sections.content:
Spring's dependency injection resolves beans **by type**. When you declare a dependency on `NotificationService`, Spring searches its container for a bean of that type and injects it. This works seamlessly — until you register two beans of the same type.

Imagine you define an `EmailNotificationService` and an `SmsNotificationService`, both implementing `NotificationService`. When another component asks for a `NotificationService`, Spring finds two candidates and has no way to decide. It throws `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException` and the application refuses to start.

`@Qualifier` solves this by attaching a name to the injection point: "I don't just want any `NotificationService` — I want the one named `smsService`." `@Primary` solves it from the other direction: "When there's ambiguity, always pick this one unless told otherwise." The two mechanisms complement each other — `@Primary` sets a sensible default, and `@Qualifier` overrides it where needed.

The common mistake is reaching for `@Qualifier` on every injection point instead of asking why you have multiple beans of the same type in the first place. Two or three implementations of the same interface scattered across one class is often a sign the class is doing too much, or that a Strategy or Factory pattern would be cleaner.

questions.title: Circular Dependencies
questions.question: What is a circular dependency in Spring and how do you resolve it?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Definition:** A depends on B, B depends on A — Spring can't resolve the cycle
- **Constructor injection fails fast:** Spring detects and throws at startup
- **`@Lazy` as a workaround:** defer one bean's initialization to break the cycle
- **Root fix:** redesign to eliminate the cycle — extract shared logic to a third class
- **Red flag:** recommending field injection to avoid the error — it hides the problem, not fixes it

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A circular dependency occurs when bean A depends on bean B and bean B depends on bean A. With constructor injection, Spring detects this at startup and throws a `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException` — which is actually good behaviour because it forces you to fix the design.

The right fix is always a design change: extract the shared logic both classes need into a third class, so A depends on C and B depends on C, breaking the cycle. This is usually a sign that responsibilities are poorly separated.

If you can't refactor immediately, `@Lazy` on one of the injection points defers the creation of that dependency until it's first accessed, breaking the circular chain. But this is a workaround, not a solution — lazy beans create harder-to-debug issues like NullPointerExceptions that appear at runtime instead of startup.

sections.title: The Dependency Cycle That Kills Your Application at Startup
sections.content:
Circular dependencies are one of the few Spring problems that feel impossible the first time you encounter them. Your application worked yesterday, someone adds a new `@Autowired` field, and suddenly Spring refuses to start with a `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException`. The stack trace is long, the error message mentions "currently in creation," and the root cause isn't where you'd expect.

The problem is structural: Bean A needs Bean B to be constructed, but Bean B needs Bean A to be constructed. Neither can be created first. With constructor injection, Spring detects this immediately — it's building A, discovers it needs B, starts building B, discovers it needs A (which is already being built), and the cycle is unresolvable.

What makes circular dependencies insidious is that they can **hide for months**. Field and setter injection used to allow them silently — Spring would inject a partially-constructed reference, and everything appeared to work until someone relied on a field that wasn't set yet. Starting with Spring Boot 2.6, circular references are prohibited by default even for setter injection. That's a deliberate choice: the cycle is always a design problem, even when Spring can technically work around it.

The most common mistake is switching from constructor to field injection to "fix" the error. This doesn't fix anything — it hides the structural problem behind a reflection hack.

sections.title: What the Cycle Looks Like in Practice
Finding Where to Break the Cycle
sections.content:
The stack trace tells you which beans are involved, but it doesn't tell you **where the cycle should be broken**. To find that, ask: which dependency direction is the weaker one? One of the two directions was added as an afterthought — it's the one that crosses a responsibility boundary.

In the example above, `OrderService → InventoryService` is natural: orders need to check and reserve inventory. But `InventoryService → OrderService` is suspicious — why does inventory management need to know about order retry logic? The stock replenishment notification is the weaker link. That's where you break the cycle.

Three signals that point to the right break point:

- One direction was added significantly later than the other
- One direction only calls a single method from the other service
- One direction crosses a domain boundary (inventory triggering order logic)

Spring Boot 2.6+ prohibits circular references by default. If you see `spring.main.allow-circular-references=true` in a codebase, treat it as tech debt — someone postponed the redesign. To debug which beans form the cycle, the startup error message lists them explicitly: "The dependencies of some of the beans in the application context form a cycle: orderService → inventoryService → orderService." Follow that chain to identify the weakest link.

questions.title: Bean Scopes
questions.question: What are the different bean scopes in Spring?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Singleton (default):** one instance per Spring container — shared across all callers
- **Prototype:** new instance on every `getBean()` call
- **Web scopes:** `request`, `session`, `application` — one per HTTP request/session/context
- **Thread safety:** singleton beans must be stateless or thread-safe — this is critical
- **Red flag:** not knowing singleton is thread-shared and ignoring thread safety implications

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Spring provides five built-in bean scopes. Singleton — the default — creates one instance per Spring container. Every time the bean is injected or retrieved, you get the same object. This means singleton beans must be stateless or thread-safe, because multiple threads access the same instance concurrently.

Prototype creates a new instance every time the bean is requested. Spring creates it and hands it off — it doesn't manage the lifecycle after creation, so you're responsible for cleanup.

For web applications, three additional scopes are available. Request creates a new instance for each HTTP request, disposed when the request ends. Session creates one per HTTP session, lasting the session's lifetime. Application creates one per `ServletContext`, shared across all sessions — similar to singleton but scoped to the web application.

The most common real-world issue is putting mutable state in a singleton bean — like a per-user counter — and getting race conditions under load.

sections.title: Why Mutable State in a Singleton Bean Becomes a Race Condition
sections.content:
Every Spring bean has a scope that controls how many instances exist and how long they live. The default — **singleton** — means one instance per Spring container, shared across every thread, every request, every user. Most developers know this intellectually but don't internalize what it means: if your singleton service has a mutable field, every concurrent request reads and writes the same variable without synchronization.

This is the most common scope-related bug in Spring applications. A developer adds a `private int counter` field to a `@Service` class, increments it per request, and everything looks fine in testing — because testing usually means one request at a time. In production, under 200 concurrent requests, the counter produces nonsensical values because `counter++` is not atomic. The field belongs on the request, not the bean.

**Prototype** scope creates a fresh instance on every injection or `getBean()` call. It's the opposite extreme: no sharing, no thread-safety concerns, but also no lifecycle management after creation — Spring doesn't track prototype beans after handing them out, so `@PreDestroy` callbacks never fire.

Web scopes — **request**, **session**, and **application** — sit between these extremes, scoping bean lifetime to an HTTP request, an HTTP session, or the entire `ServletContext`. They require a web-aware application context and a scoped proxy when injected into a singleton, because the singleton outlives every request and session.

sections.title: Scope Lifecycle and Thread Safety at a Glance
sections.content:
Choosing the right scope requires understanding not just the instance count, but the lifecycle guarantees and thread-safety implications. This table covers the five built-in scopes across the dimensions that matter in production.

| Scope | Instances | Lifetime | Thread-safe? | `@PreDestroy` called? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| singleton | 1 per container | Application lifetime | Your responsibility | Yes |
| prototype | New per injection | Until garbage collected | Yes (not shared) | No |
| request | 1 per HTTP request | Single request | Yes (one thread) | Yes |
| session | 1 per HTTP session | Session lifetime | Potentially shared (Ajax) | Yes |
| application | 1 per `ServletContext` | Application lifetime | Your responsibility | Yes |

The prototype row is the one that surprises developers: Spring does **not** call `@PreDestroy` on prototype beans. Once Spring hands you the instance, it's your responsibility to clean up. If your prototype bean holds a database connection or file handle, you must close it explicitly — Spring won't do it for you.

questions.title: @Value and Property Injection
questions.question: How does @Value work for injecting properties into Spring beans?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **SpEL and property placeholder:** `@Value("${property.key}")` vs `@Value("#{expression}")`
- **Default values:** `@Value("${key:default}")`
- **Type conversion:** Spring converts String to int, boolean, Duration automatically
- **`@ConfigurationProperties` is preferred for groups of related properties**
- **Red flag:** not knowing the colon syntax for defaults — common source of startup failures

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
`@Value` injects values from property sources into Spring beans. The most common form is `@Value("${property.key}")` using the property placeholder syntax — Spring looks up `property.key` in the environment and injects its value. If the key doesn't exist, the application fails to start with a `IllegalArgumentException`.

You can provide a default with the colon syntax: `@Value("${property.key:default-value}")`. If the key is missing, `default-value` is used instead of failing.

For injecting multiple related properties, `@ConfigurationProperties` is a better approach. It binds a group of `app.*` properties to a POJO, gives you type safety, and supports validation. `@Value` is fine for one or two isolated values; `@ConfigurationProperties` is better for structured configuration groups.

sections.title: Why Missing Properties Crash Your Application — and the One-Character Fix
sections.content:
`@Value` is the simplest way to get external configuration into a Spring bean — and it's also the most common source of startup failures for teams that don't know one syntax detail. When you write `@Value("${api.url}")` and `api.url` isn't defined in any property source, Spring doesn't inject null or an empty string. It throws `IllegalArgumentException` and your application refuses to start.

The fix is a single colon: `@Value("${api.url:}")` provides an empty string default. `@Value("${api.url:https://fallback.example.com}")` provides a meaningful fallback. This **colon syntax** is the difference between an application that explodes on missing configuration and one that degrades gracefully.

But `@Value` has a deeper scaling problem beyond defaults. It works fine for one or two properties, but past three related values — a URL, a timeout, a retry count — it becomes scattered and untestable. Each property is injected independently, validated nowhere, and documented nowhere. For structured configuration, `@ConfigurationProperties` is the proper tool: it binds a prefix to a POJO, validates at startup, and generates IDE auto-completion metadata.

The decision is simple: **`@Value` for isolated one-off values** (a feature flag, a secret key). **`@ConfigurationProperties` for anything with a prefix and more than two properties.**

questions.title: @Autowired Internals
questions.question: How does @Autowired work internally in Spring?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **`AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor`:** the component that processes `@Autowired`
- **Resolution order:** type → qualifier → name
- **`required = false`:** injection is optional — field stays null if no matching bean
- **`BeanPostProcessor` hook:** fires after bean construction but before it's returned to callers
- **Red flag:** thinking `@Autowired` is just magic — not knowing the `BeanPostProcessor` mechanism

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
`@Autowired` is processed by `AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor`, which implements Spring's `BeanPostProcessor` interface. After a bean is instantiated, Spring calls each registered `BeanPostProcessor`. The `AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor` scans the bean for `@Autowired` annotations — on fields, setters, or constructors — and performs the injection.

For each injection point, Spring resolves the dependency by type first. If multiple beans of the same type exist, it narrows down by qualifier. If there's still ambiguity, it tries to match by the field name or parameter name against bean names.

By default, `@Autowired` injection is required — if Spring can't find a matching bean, it throws `NoSuchBeanDefinitionException` at startup. Setting `required = false` makes the injection optional, leaving the field null if no bean is available.

sections.title: The Post-Processor That Makes @Autowired Look Like Magic
sections.content:
Most developers treat `@Autowired` as built-in Spring syntax — something the framework "just knows" how to handle. In reality, `@Autowired` has no special status in Spring's core. It's processed by a regular component called `AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor`, which implements the same `BeanPostProcessor` interface available to any developer. Understanding this mechanism demystifies not just `@Autowired`, but every annotation-driven feature in Spring.

When Spring creates a bean, it doesn't hand it back immediately. It passes the raw instance through every registered **BeanPostProcessor** — a pipeline of components that can inspect, modify, or even replace the bean. `AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor` is one processor in this pipeline. It uses reflection to find fields, methods, and constructors annotated with `@Autowired` (and also `@Inject` and `@Value`), resolves each dependency from the `BeanFactory`, and injects them before the bean is considered "ready."

This means `@Autowired` injection happens **after** the constructor runs but **before** `@PostConstruct`. If you access an `@Autowired` field inside the constructor, it's `null` — the post-processor hasn't run yet. This timing mistake is the most common source of NullPointerExceptions during bean initialization, and it's exactly why constructor injection exists: constructor parameters are available inside the constructor by definition.

sections.title: Phase 1: Scanning the Bean for Injection Points
sections.content:
After the bean's constructor finishes, `AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor` reflects on the bean's class to discover injection metadata. It searches for three things: fields annotated with `@Autowired`, `@Inject`, or `@Value`; setter methods carrying the same annotations; and constructors marked with `@Autowired`.

For constructor injection with a single constructor, Spring 4.3+ automatically treats the sole constructor as an injection point — no `@Autowired` annotation required. This convention removed the last piece of boilerplate that made field injection look appealing.

The processor **caches** injection metadata per class, so reflection only happens once per bean type, not once per bean instance. For prototype-scoped beans that get created many times, this caching is critical for performance. The metadata includes not just which fields need injection, but also whether each injection point is required or optional, what qualifier it carries, and what type it expects.

sections.title: Phase 2: Resolving Each Dependency by Type, Then by Name
sections.content:
For each injection point discovered in Phase 1, the processor asks the `BeanFactory` to resolve a dependency. The resolution follows a specific algorithm that developers must understand to debug ambiguity errors.

Spring first matches **by type**. If exactly one bean of the required type exists in the container, it's injected immediately. If none exist and `required = true` (the default), Spring throws `NoSuchBeanDefinitionException` at startup.

When multiple beans of the same type exist, Spring narrows the candidates through a priority chain: first it checks for a `@Qualifier` annotation on the injection point. If a qualifier is present and matches a bean, that bean wins. Next, it looks for a `@Primary` bean among the candidates. Finally, it attempts **name matching** — if your field is named `emailService` and a bean with that name exists among the candidates, Spring picks it.

The full priority order is: **@Qualifier → @Primary → name match → failure**. The name-matching fallback is convenient but fragile — rename the field and the resolution silently changes, potentially injecting a completely different bean. Understanding this sequence is essential for debugging `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException`, where the error message lists the candidates and you can trace the algorithm to see where resolution fell through.

sections.title: Phase 3: Injecting via Reflection and the required Flag
sections.content:
Once a dependency is resolved, the processor injects it via reflection. For fields, it calls `Field.setAccessible(true)` and sets the value directly — bypassing access modifiers entirely. This is why `@Autowired` works on `private` fields, and it's also why field injection is impossible without reflection: there's no framework-free path to set a private field from outside the class.

For methods (setter injection), the processor invokes the method with the resolved bean as an argument. For constructors, the dependency resolution actually happens earlier — during instantiation itself, handled by `SmartInstantiationAwareBeanPostProcessor` — so the bean is constructed with its dependencies already available.

The **`required` attribute** controls what happens on resolution failure. With `required = true` (the default), a missing dependency is a fatal startup error. With `required = false`, the injection point is skipped — the field stays `null`, the setter isn't called. Since Spring 4.3, `Optional<T>` provides a better alternative: the field is always injected (never null itself), and you use `Optional.ifPresent()` to handle the absence safely and explicitly.

It's processed by a regular component called AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor, which implements the same BeanPostProcessor interface available to any developer. Understanding this mechanism demystifies not just @Autowired, but every annotation-driven feature in Spring. When Spring creates a bean, it doesn't hand it back immediately. It passes the raw instance through every registered BeanPostProcessor — a pipeline of components that can inspect, modify, or even replace.

This convention removed the last piece of boilerplate that made field injection look appealing.
The processor caches injection metadata per class, so reflection only happens once per bean type, not once per bean instance.

questions.title: @ConfigurationProperties
questions.question: What is @ConfigurationProperties and when should you use it instead of @Value?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Type-safe property binding:** binds a property prefix to a POJO
- **Advantages over `@Value`:** validation, IDE support, refactoring safety
- **`@EnableConfigurationProperties` or `@Component`:** how you register it
- **Supports nested objects and lists natively**
- **Red flag:** not knowing the validation integration — `@Validated` + JSR-303 on properties

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
`@ConfigurationProperties` binds a prefix of properties to a Java class. Instead of injecting each property individually with `@Value`, you define a class where each field maps to a property key under the prefix. Spring binds all matching properties to the POJO at startup.

The advantages over `@Value` are significant. You get type safety — a property declared as `Duration timeout` correctly parses `10s` or `PT10S` without conversion code. You get IDE auto-completion in `application.properties` when the class is registered in `spring-configuration-metadata.json`. You get validation by adding `@Validated` and JSR-303 annotations like `@NotNull` and `@Min`. And you can refactor field names in your IDE and have them update correctly.

Use `@Value` for a single isolated value. Use `@ConfigurationProperties` for any grouped configuration with 3+ properties.

sections.title: Why Scattering @Value Across 20 Classes Becomes Unmaintainable
sections.content:
The moment your application has more than a handful of configuration properties, `@Value` starts to hurt. Each property is injected independently into whichever class needs it. There's no single place to see all the properties your mail subsystem requires. There's no validation — a missing `mail.host` surfaces as a NullPointerException deep in a service call, not as a clear startup error. And there's no documentation — new team members grep the codebase for `@Value` annotations to discover what properties exist.

**`@ConfigurationProperties`** solves all three problems by binding an entire property prefix to a dedicated Java class. Every field in the class maps to a property under the prefix. The class becomes the single source of truth for that subsystem's configuration: what's required, what has defaults, what types are expected, and what validation rules apply.

The mechanism is binding, not injection. Spring doesn't process individual annotations — it takes the `mail.*` properties from the environment and maps them onto the POJO's fields using setter methods or constructor binding. Nested objects, lists, maps, and `Duration` types all work naturally without SpEL expressions or custom converters.

The decisive advantage is **startup validation**. Add `@Validated` to the class and JSR-303 annotations to the fields, and Spring validates the entire configuration group at startup. A missing required property or an out-of-range port number fails immediately with a message naming the exact property and the violated constraint — compare that to `@Value("${mail.port}")`, which gives you a generic `IllegalArgumentException` with no indication of valid values.

sections.title: @Value vs @ConfigurationProperties: When Each Makes Sense
sections.content:
The choice between `@Value` and `@ConfigurationProperties` depends on how many related properties you're managing and whether you need validation. This table covers the dimensions that matter in real projects.

| Concern | `@Value` | `@ConfigurationProperties` |
|---|---|---|
| Use case | 1–2 isolated properties | Grouped properties with a prefix |
| Type safety | Manual — `String` by default | Automatic — binds to field types |
| Defaults | `${key:default}` colon syntax | Field initializers in Java |
| Validation | None built-in | `@Validated` + JSR-303 annotations |
| IDE support | No auto-completion | Auto-completion via generated metadata |
| Nested objects | Requires SpEL workarounds | Native support |
| Refactoring | Rename-fragile (string-based keys) | Rename-safe (Java fields) |
| Documentation | Scattered across many classes | One class per config group |

The crossover point is clear: once you have **three or more related properties under a common prefix**, `@ConfigurationProperties` pays for itself in validation, discoverability, and maintainability. Below that threshold, `@Value` with a sensible default is simpler and perfectly adequate.

questions.title: Lazy Initialization
questions.question: How does @Lazy work for bean initialization in Spring?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Default is eager:** singleton beans created at startup
- **`@Lazy` defers creation:** bean created on first use, not at startup
- **Spring Boot `spring.main.lazy-initialization=true`:** global lazy init
- **Trade-off:** faster startup, but first request is slower and errors surface at runtime not startup
- **Red flag:** using `@Lazy` everywhere as a startup optimization — errors deferred to runtime

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
By default, Spring creates all singleton beans at startup. This means you detect configuration errors and missing dependencies immediately when the application starts — which is a good thing.

`@Lazy` defers a bean's creation until it's first requested. Annotate a bean class or a `@Bean` method with `@Lazy`, and Spring creates a proxy placeholder at startup. The actual bean is created the first time any code calls a method on it.

Lazy initialization speeds up startup time, which is valuable during development (faster restart loops) or for rarely-used beans. Spring Boot 2.2+ added `spring.main.lazy-initialization=true` to make all beans lazy globally. The trade-off is that errors in lazy beans — missing configuration, failed database connections — appear at request time instead of startup, making them harder to catch in deployment checks.

sections.title: Faster Startup, Deferred Failures: The Trade-Off Behind @Lazy
sections.content:
Spring's default behavior is to create all singleton beans at startup. This is slow — a large application might take 30 seconds just to wire everything — but it's **intentionally** slow. Eager initialization catches configuration errors, missing dependencies, and broken database connections the moment you deploy. Your health check returns healthy only after every bean has been successfully created.

`@Lazy` flips this contract. A lazy bean isn't created until something actually calls a method on it. Spring creates a lightweight CGLIB proxy at startup — a placeholder that looks like the real bean — and defers actual construction to first use. This makes startup faster, but it moves errors from deployment time to request time.

The trade-off seems straightforward until you consider what "first use" means in production. Your application starts, passes health checks, gets registered in the load balancer, and begins receiving traffic. The first request that touches the lazy bean triggers construction. If construction fails — a database is unreachable, a property is misconfigured — that request gets an exception. Worse, every monitoring system already thinks the application is healthy.

Global lazy initialization via `spring.main.lazy-initialization=true` amplifies this risk: **every** bean's construction errors are deferred. This is valuable for development — shaving 20 seconds off restart cycles matters when you're iterating — but dangerous in production unless paired with a warmup strategy. The one place `@Lazy` is genuinely useful beyond development is breaking circular dependencies: injecting a proxy instead of a real bean allows both beans to finish construction, deferring the cycle to first method call.

questions.title: Conditional Bean Registration
questions.question: How do you conditionally register beans using @Conditional annotations?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **`@ConditionalOnProperty`:** register bean based on a property value
- **`@ConditionalOnClass`:** register if a class is on the classpath
- **`@ConditionalOnMissingBean`:** register only if no other bean of the type exists (auto-config pattern)
- **`@ConditionalOnBean`:** register only if another bean exists
- **Red flag:** not knowing these are the foundation of Spring Boot auto-configuration

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Spring provides a family of `@Conditional` annotations for registering beans based on runtime or classpath conditions. These are the foundation of Spring Boot's auto-configuration — every auto-configuration class uses them to register beans only when appropriate conditions are met.

`@ConditionalOnProperty` registers the bean only when a property exists or has a specific value — great for feature flags. `@ConditionalOnClass` registers the bean only when a specific class is on the classpath — how Spring Boot detects that you're using, say, Redis, and auto-configures it. `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` registers the bean only if no other bean of that type is already registered — this is what allows you to override Spring Boot defaults by declaring your own bean.

These annotations are evaluated during context refresh, before beans are instantiated, so the conditions are efficient.

sections.title: How Spring Boot Decides What to Auto-Configure — and How You Override It
sections.content:
Every Spring Boot application starts with hundreds of auto-configuration classes — `DataSourceAutoConfiguration`, `RedisAutoConfiguration`, `JpaAutoConfiguration`, and more. Yet only a few actually create beans. The rest silently back off. The mechanism behind this selective activation is the `@Conditional` annotation family, and understanding it answers the question every developer eventually asks: "How does Spring Boot know I'm using Redis?"

The answer is **classpath detection**. `RedisAutoConfiguration` is annotated with `@ConditionalOnClass(RedisOperations.class)`. If `spring-data-redis` is on your classpath — because you added the starter dependency — the class `RedisOperations` exists, the condition passes, and Spring Boot configures Redis. If you haven't added the dependency, the class doesn't exist, the condition fails, and the entire auto-configuration is skipped without error.

This same mechanism lets you override Spring Boot's defaults. Auto-configuration beans are annotated with `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`. If you declare your own `DataSource` bean in a `@Configuration` class, Spring Boot's `DataSourceAutoConfiguration` detects it and backs off — your bean wins. This isn't magic; it's a simple condition check: "Does a bean of this type already exist? If yes, don't create mine."

Understanding `@Conditional` annotations transforms you from someone who pastes Spring Boot configuration from Stack Overflow to someone who understands **why** that configuration works and can debug it when it doesn't.

questions.title: Component Scanning
questions.question: How does Spring's component scanning work?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Classpath scanning for stereotypes:** `@Component`, `@Service`, `@Repository`, `@Controller`
- **`@SpringBootApplication` includes `@ComponentScan`:** scans the package and subpackages
- **Exclusions and inclusions:** `includeFilters`, `excludeFilters`
- **`@ComponentScan(basePackages=...)`:** scan additional packages outside the default
- **Red flag:** not knowing the default scan package is where `@SpringBootApplication` lives

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Component scanning is Spring's mechanism for automatically discovering and registering beans without explicit `@Bean` declarations. It scans the classpath for classes annotated with stereotype annotations — `@Component`, `@Service`, `@Repository`, `@Controller` — and registers them as Spring beans.

`@SpringBootApplication` includes `@ComponentScan`, which by default scans the package where your main application class lives and all subpackages. This is why the convention is to put your main class at the root of your package — `com.example.myapp.Application` — so all packages under `com.example.myapp` are scanned automatically.

If you have classes in a different package — maybe a shared library — you add `@ComponentScan(basePackages = {"com.example.myapp", "com.shared.library"})` to include that package. Or `@ComponentScan(basePackageClasses = SharedConfig.class)` for type-safe package declaration.

sections.title: The Invisible Walk Through Your Classpath That Builds the Bean Registry
sections.content:
Think of component scanning as Spring walking through your project's compiled classes with a flashlight, looking for specific annotations. It opens every `.class` file under certain packages, checks if the class carries a stereotype annotation — `@Component`, `@Service`, `@Repository`, `@Controller` — and if it does, Spring registers a `BeanDefinition` for it. The bean is then created during context refresh, just like beans declared with `@Bean` methods.

The critical detail most developers miss is **where the walk starts**. `@SpringBootApplication` includes `@ComponentScan` with no explicit base package, which means Spring uses the package of the annotated class as the root. If your main class lives in `com.example.app`, Spring scans `com.example.app` and every sub-package recursively. A class in `com.example.shared` is invisible — it's outside the scan root.

This is why the Spring Boot convention is to place your main application class at the **root of your package hierarchy**. It's not just organization — it's the scan boundary. Breaking this convention is the number one reason developers find that their `@Service` or `@Repository` classes aren't being detected, leading to `NoSuchBeanDefinitionException` for dependencies that clearly exist in the source code.

Stereotype annotations are not all equal, even though they're all detected by scanning. `@Repository` adds automatic exception translation — it wraps data access exceptions into Spring's `DataAccessException` hierarchy. `@Controller` activates request mapping detection. `@Service` adds no extra behavior — it's purely semantic, a documentation signal that the class contains business logic.

sections.title: From .class File to BeanDefinition: What Happens During the Scan
sections.content:
During context refresh, `ClassPathBeanDefinitionScanner` walks the file system or JAR entries under each base package. For each `.class` file, it reads the bytecode metadata using ASM (a bytecode analysis library), **not** full class loading. This distinction is important for performance — Spring doesn't load every class into the JVM just to check if it has `@Component`. It reads raw bytecode, which is significantly faster for large classpaths with hundreds of JARs.

When a matching class is found, Spring creates a **BeanDefinition** — a metadata object describing the bean's class, scope, lazy flag, dependency information, and init/destroy methods. This definition is registered in the `BeanDefinitionRegistry`, but no object is created yet. Actual instantiation happens later, during `finishBeanFactoryInitialization`, after all definitions are collected and `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` implementations have had a chance to modify them.

This two-phase process — scan then create — is what makes `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` possible. It can modify bean definitions between scanning and instantiation: changing scopes, adding property values, or even registering entirely new definitions that weren't in the original scan. The scan is just the first half of the story.
